replacement: “Hold on. Look at the night. See how dark it is, the clouds, the wind that’s picked up. I was hiding under that willow, waiting for you. And I swear by God above, I suddenly thought: why drag on in misery any longer? What is there left to wait for? Here’s a willow, here’s a handkerchief, here’s a shirt. In a minute I can twist them into a rope, and I have my suspenders too. Why go on weighing down the earth and shaming it with my filthy presence? And then I heard you coming—heavens, it was as if something had suddenly flown down to me. So there is someone I love after all! Here he is, my dear little brother, the one I love more than anyone in the world, the only one I love in the world. And at that moment I loved you so much, so much, that I thought, ‘I’ll throw myself on his neck this instant.’ Then a stupid notion came over me: play a joke on you, give you a scare. So I shouted that idiotic ‘Your money!’ Forgive the clowning—it was nonsense, and there’s nothing improper in my soul.... Damn it all, tell me what happened. What did she say? Hit me, crush me, show me no mercy! Was she furious?”
“Impossible!” he cried. “You’re raving! Grushenka with her?”

“Brother, you don’t seem to have noticed how badly you insulted Katerina Ivanovna by telling Grushenka about that day. And Grushenka threw it in her face just now: that she had gone to gentlemen in secret to sell her beauty! Brother, what insult could be worse than that?”

“Yes, maybe I did tell Grushenka about that ‘fatal day,’ as Katya calls it. Yes, I told her, I remember it now! It was at Mokroe. I was drunk, the gypsies were singing.... But I was sobbing. I was sobbing then, on my knees, praying to Katya’s image, and Grushenka understood. She understood everything then. I remember, she cried herself.... Damn it all! But it’s bound to be like that now.... Then she cried, and now it’s ‘the dagger in the heart’! That’s women for you.”

Now he was rather puzzled and did not know whom to believe. The evening before, he had visited Father Ferapont in his separate cell behind the apiary, and the visit had left him deeply impressed and awed. This Father Ferapont was the aged monk, devoted to fasting and silence, who has been mentioned already as opposed to Father Zossima and to the whole institution of “elders,” which he held to be a harmful and frivolous novelty. He was a formidable opponent, although his practice of silence meant he hardly spoke to anyone. He was formidable because a number of monks shared his feelings entirely, and many visitors saw him as a great saint and ascetic, even though they had no doubt he was crazy. Yet it was precisely his craziness that drew them.
